text:
Garlic.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer

Garlic is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves, usually planted in autumn for a summer harvest. Flavour varies with the variety, from mild cloves to strongly pungent types. Young plants tolerate very cold winter weather, fit conveniently into the garden after summer crops, and are lifted early enough to be followed by French beans, late brassicas or autumn salads.

Quick facts
Plant cloves

Oct–Dec. Jan–Mar for suitable spring varieties.

Harvest

Jun – Aug

Ready in

Summer; ~8–9 months from autumn planting, less from spring

Yield (10 ft row)

About 20 ordinary garlic bulbs or 10 elephant garlic bulbs.

Clove depth

Cover tips with 1 in. of soil. Plant deeper only on light ground.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Plant spacing

Ordinary garlic: 6 in. apart; elephant garlic: about 12 in. apart

Recommended varieties
SOFTNECK
Solent Wight

A softneck garlic well suited to UK gardens and storage. A useful first choice for a dependable household crop.

SOFTNECK
Germidour

A softneck garlic with purple-marked skins. A familiar alternative for gardeners wanting large, useful bulbs.

Carcassonne Wight

A hardneck garlic providing an alternative to softneck types. It also produces edible flower stems, known as scapes.

LEEK RELATIVE; LARGE MILD CLOVES
Elephant

Produces very large, mild cloves. Grow as a separate culinary option; it is a leek relative rather than true garlic.

HARDNECK
Spanish Roja

A strongly flavoured hardneck with thin skins. Remove tender flower stems as buds form; check specialist suppliers for planting stock.

Key risks
White rot

White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.

Allium leaf miner

Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.

Rust

Orange pustules appear on allium leaves, especially leeks and garlic.

Birds or frost lifting cloves

Cloves lifted by birds or frost.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
56
ONION FAMILY

Plant healthy cloves in good drainage.

Named planting stock gives a more predictable crop than kitchen bulbs.

Lift and dry bulbs at maturity.

Careful handling and thorough drying help garlic keep.

Soil & preparation
Choose an open, sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. Add compost or well-rotted manure, but avoid stagnant winter wet.
A compost top-dressing helps retain moisture; keep it clear of emerging shoots.
Sowing & planting
Set a clove upright
Cover the clove tip
Plant cloves 

Break up a healthy bulb just before planting. Use the largest outside cloves. Set each with its point upwards, cover the tip and firm the soil.

On wet ground 

Start cloves individually in modules under cover. Plant out the rooted cloves when the bed is workable.

Looking after the crop
Keep weeds down through winter and spring. Slow winter shoots are normal: cold can check visible growth until roots and leaves grow strongly in spring.
Water roots in dry weather while bulbs grow; stop as mature foliage yellows. Cut tender hardneck scapes once buds form. Use tender scapes raw or cooked. Softneck garlic normally produces no flower stalk and usually stores longer than hardneck types.
Harvesting & storage
Use green garlic whole in late spring. Check mature bulbs from June and lift as foliage yellows, before skins break down.
Loosen soil and lift gently to avoid bruising. Brush off dirt without washing. Cure for 2–4 weeks in dry, airy, rainproof shelter below 86°F; trim only when leaves and skins are dry. Store cool and dry.
Severe rust can bring harvest forward. Elephant garlic needs more room and a longer season; judge maturity from the plant and bulb.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
White rot	White mould and decay at bulb bases.	Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected ground.
Allium leaf miner	White puncture rows; internal maggots or pupae.	Mesh during fly activity; remove infested plants and debris.
Rust	Orange pustules; leaves yellow early.	Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; clear affected debris.
Birds or frost lifting cloves	Cloves are pulled up or frost-heaved.	Cover tips at planting; firm and replant lifted cloves.
Poor storage	Bulbs rot or sprout in store.	Lift on time, handle gently and dry thoroughly.
Stem & bulb eelworm	Swollen, distorted growth; soft bases.	Confirm diagnosis; remove plants and avoid moving affected soil.
Final tips

Softneck types usually store longer; use hardnecks earlier and enjoy their edible scapes.

Elephant garlic is a leek relative with large, mild cloves, so give it extra room.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
